analysis.one_liner: Restores state consumer-protection laws over national banks and federal savings associations.
analysis.headline: S. 1502 was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in July 2005, never drew a cosponsor, and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In the mid-2000s, the Treasury regulator for national banks issued rules shielding those banks from most state consumer-protection laws, meaning state laws against deceptive lending, fraud, and abusive foreclosure or collection practices generally did not apply to them. This bill would have reversed that: state consumer laws of general application, stronger state predatory-lending rules, and state attorneys general's power to sue banks on behalf of residents would all apply to national banks and federal savings associations. It also required the two federal banking regulators to log every consumer complaint and report on them to Congress twice a year.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank customers and borrowers, especially people facing high-cost mortgages, foreclosure, or abusive debt collection, because they could again rely on their own state's consumer-protection and anti-fraud laws against any national bank or federal thrift, and state attorneys general could sue banks on their behalf.

how_it_helps.text: State consumer-protection laws of general application, including unfair-or-deceptive-practices and consumer-fraud laws and laws on repossession, foreclosure, and collection, would apply to national banks and federal savings associations [S2][S3].
State laws offering greater protection against high-cost predatory mortgage loans than federal law would apply to national banks and federal thrifts [S2][S3].

State attorneys general could enforce federal or state law against national banks and federal thrifts and recover damages for state residents, authority the bill says federal visitorial-power rules cannot limit [S2][S3].

A bank that uses a state law for its own benefit must accept all the related consumer protections in that state law, and a loan that was not preempted at origination does not become preempted when later sold to a national bank [S3].

The Comptroller of the Currency and the thrift regulator would have to record and monitor every consumer complaint, and report complaint counts, resolution times, and enforcement actions to Congress and post them online twice a year [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: National banks and federal savings associations, which would lose the federal preemption shield and face state consumer laws, state predatory-lending rules, and lawsuits by state attorneys general and private parties, with compliance and litigation costs likely passed on in some form to consumers.
analysis.who_pays_short: National banks and federal savings associations

drawbacks.text: Banks and their regulators argued a single national standard is simpler and cheaper than 50 different state rulebooks, and that some of the added compliance and litigation costs would show up in fees and rates charged to the same consumers the bill aims to protect [S2].
The bill leaves the interest-rate preemption national banks have long enjoyed under federal law intact, so it would not have stopped the export of high interest rates across state lines [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have handed consumers and state enforcers a meaningful check on national banks at the cost of extra compliance complexity for the banking industry. The added-fee objection is real but modest next to the core problem the bill addressed: under the preemption rules then in effect, a borrower deceived by a national bank often could not use state fraud or predatory-lending laws at all. It was a straightforward, if narrower-than-a-full-repeal, consumer-protection fix.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced and stayed there; the committee never took it up, it never got a cosponsor, and it expired when the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Corzine introduced the bill on July 26, 2005 and spoke about it on the Senate floor; it was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S1][S5].
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor at any point [S4].
The complete action record shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the initial referral [S5].

The bill would have overridden the OCC's preemption rules by applying state consumer-protection, predatory-lending, and fraud laws to national banks and federal savings associations and preserving state attorneys general enforcement power [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: National banks and federal thrifts, which kept the federal preemption shield from state consumer-protection laws, and the federal regulators whose exclusive oversight the bill would have pared back; consumers left without state-law remedies against national banks were worse off.

for.name: Sen. Jon Corzine
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it on the Senate floor.

for.name: State attorneys general
for.what_they_did: Sued and lobbied to preserve their authority to enforce state consumer laws against national banks after federal regulators asserted exclusive visitorial power.

against.name: Senate Banking Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Richard Shelby (R-AL)
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: National banking industry
against.role: National banks and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Backed the OCC preemption rules the bill would have overturned and opposed applying state consumer laws to federally chartered banks.

against.name: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
against.what_they_did: Defended its preemption rules and exclusive supervisory authority over national banks.

sides.party_line_note: No roll call was ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors, so there is no voting record of the split; the sponsor was a Democrat and the Republican-chaired Banking Committee took no action.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped away the OCC preemption shield that kept state consumer-protection, fraud, and predatory-lending laws from reaching them, and opened them to suits by state attorneys general and private borrowers. Their interest in keeping the shield ran directly against borrowers' ability to use state law.
Federal thrifts would have become subject to the same state consumer laws and predatory-lending rules as state-chartered institutions, losing a regulatory advantage over state competitors.

industries.industry: Nonbank mortgage and lending subsidiaries of national banks
industries.note: The bill clarifies that state-chartered nonbank units and agents of national banks remain fully subject to state law, closing an avenue by which lending operations moved under the federal preemption umbrella.

The bill would have expressly preserved state AG authority to enforce state and federal law against national banks and recover damages for residents, restoring an enforcement channel that had been narrowed.
